opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to the fact that right now, most leaderboards treat models as if they exist in a vacuum. You see a ranking based on accuracy or some aggregate score, and the implicit message is that the model at the top is the "best" one. But a model that needs a cluster of high-end GPUs to run isn't really comparable to one that runs on a laptop or a single consumer card. They're serving different purposes and different people.

When you don't make that distinction, you end up rewarding scale above everything else. The biggest models tend to win, so the incentive for everyone is to go bigger, use more compute, use more energy. And the trade-offs, like cost, latency, carbon footprint, and who can actually afford to deploy the thing, just disappear from the conversation.

If you group models by the hardware they need, almost like weight classes in boxing, you get a much more honest picture. You can say, "Within models that run on a single GPU, this one performs best," and that's actually useful for a developer, a startup, or a researcher at a university who doesn't have access to a data center. It also highlights the people doing really clever work on efficiency, which right now often gets overshadowed because they're being compared against models that are orders of magnitude larger.

And from a sustainability perspective, which is a lot of what I work on, it makes energy and resource use visible. If a smaller model gets you 95% of the performance for a fraction of the compute, that's important information. People should be able to make that choice consciously instead of defaulting to the biggest model because it's at the top of a list. So for me it's about making benchmarks reflect how models are actually used, and making efficiency something the field values rather than an afterthought.

r001.rationale: It says models needing a high-end GPU cluster are not comparable to models running on a laptop or consumer card because they serve different purposes and people.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot. When you look at the leaderboards, you get this single number, or maybe a handful of numbers, and the models are all lined up as if they're comparable. But a model that needs eight H100s to run inference and a model that fits on a single consumer GPU, or on your laptop, those are not the same thing, even if they score within a point of each other on MMLU or whatever the benchmark of the week is.

And I think that matters for a few reasons. The first one, which is the one I care about most, is energy and environmental impact. We did this work on the Energy Star AI project where we actually measured the energy consumption of models on a bunch of tasks, and the spread is enormous. You can have models that are orders of magnitude apart in how much energy they use per query, and that's completely invisible on a standard accuracy leaderboard. So if you're a practitioner choosing a model, you're being pushed toward the biggest thing at the top of the list, when a much smaller model might get you ninety-five percent of the way there for a fraction of the cost and the footprint.

The second reason is access. If the only models that are "state of the art" require a data center to run, then the benchmark is implicitly saying that only people with data centers get to do state-of-the-art work. And that's not great for researchers, for people in the Global South, for small companies, for anyone who isn't one of five labs. Distinguishing by hardware tier, like saying here's the best model that runs on a phone, here's the best model that runs on one GPU, here's the best that runs on a cluster, it makes the comparison fair. It's a bit like weight classes in boxing. You don't put the heavyweight in the ring with the flyweight and then call it a competition.

And honestly, the third reason is that it would change the incentives. Right now the incentive is just scale, scale, scale, because that's what moves the number. If leaderboards rewarded efficiency, if you got credit for doing well within a hardware budget, I think we'd see a lot more creative work on distillation, quantization, architecture, all the stuff that actually makes AI more sustainable and more deployable. The benchmark shapes the field, so I'd rather it shape it toward something a bit more reasonable than just "who has the most compute."

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes models by hardware tier and discusses who can access them, but it does not clearly state that different hardware requirements correspond to different use cases.

astra-6.text:
Because when we compare models only on accuracy, we’re leaving out a really important part of the picture: what does it take to actually run them? A model that you can run on your laptop and a model that needs a whole server full of GPUs might get similar scores, but they’re very different in terms of who can use them and at what cost.

I’d like to see benchmarks make those trade-offs visible. If you have a certain amount of memory or a certain compute budget, what’s the best performance you can get? And if you use a lot more resources, how much better does the model actually become? That lets people choose something that fits their needs, rather than treating the highest score as the only thing that matters.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts laptop-runnable models with models that need a GPU server, explaining that they differ in who can use them and that people should choose based on their needs. This communicates that different hardware requirements suit different use cases.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a benchmark score doesn’t tell you what it takes to actually use a model. If one model needs a whole server full of GPUs and another can run on your laptop, those are very different propositions, even if their scores are similar. They have different costs, energy requirements, and implications for who can access them.

I’d like to see benchmarks compare models within those kinds of hardware categories, so you can ask, “What’s the best model I can run with the resources I have?” And then we can recognize efficiency as an achievement, too. Getting a little more accuracy by using a lot more compute isn’t necessarily the most useful progress for everyone.

r001.rationale: The response says models with different hardware needs are different propositions and should be compared by hardware category, but it does not clearly state that they correspond to different use cases.
